Arrays & Hashing.title: Mastering Arrays & Hashing
Arrays & Hashing.content:
## 1. Arrays in Java

Arrays are the most fundamental data structure. In Java, arrays are objects stored in contiguous memory.

### Declaration & Initialization
```java
int[] arr = new int[5];           // Size 5, default 0s
int[] arr = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};      // Direct init
int[][] matrix = new int[3][3];   // 2D array
```

### Key Properties
- **Fixed Size**: Cannot resize after creation
- **Zero-indexed**: First element at index 0
- **Homogeneous**: All elements same type

---

## 2. HashMap & HashSet

### HashMap (Key-Value Store)
```java
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("apple", 5);
map.get("apple");           // Returns 5
map.getOrDefault("x", 0);   // Returns 0 if key missing
map.containsKey("apple");   // true
map.keySet();               // All keys
map.values();               // All values
```

### HashSet (Unique Elements)
```java
Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(1);
set.contains(1);  // true
set.remove(1);
```

---

## 3. Common Patterns

### Frequency Counter
```java
Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (char c : str.toCharArray()) {
    freq.put(c, freq.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
}
```

### Two Sum Pattern
```java
Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    int complement = target - nums[i];
    if (seen.containsKey(complement)) {
        return new int[]{seen.get(complement), i};
    }
    seen.put(nums[i], i);
}
```

---

## 4. Interview Questions

**Q: HashMap vs Hashtable?**
A: HashMap is not synchronized (faster), allows null keys. Hashtable is synchronized (thread-safe), no nulls.

**Q: How does HashMap handle collisions?**
A: Uses chaining (LinkedList). Java 8+ converts to Red-Black Tree when chain > 8.

**Q: Time complexity of HashMap operations?**
A: O(1) average for get/put. O(n) worst case with bad hash function.

Stack.title: Stack Data Structure
Stack.content:
## 1. Stack Basics

**LIFO** - Last In, First Out

```java
Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();
stack.push(1);      // Add to top
stack.pop();        // Remove from top
stack.peek();       // View top without removing
stack.isEmpty();    // Check if empty
stack.size();       // Number of elements
```

---

## 2. Monotonic Stack

A stack that maintains elements in sorted order (increasing or decreasing).

### Next Greater Element
```java
int[] result = new int[nums.length];
Arrays.fill(result, -1);
Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();  // Store indices

for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    while (!stack.isEmpty() && nums[stack.peek()] < nums[i]) {
        result[stack.pop()] = nums[i];
    }
    stack.push(i);
}
```

---

## 3. Common Applications

| Problem | Technique |
|---------|----------|
| Valid Parentheses | Match opening with closing |
| Daily Temperatures | Monotonic decreasing stack |
| Largest Rectangle in Histogram | Monotonic increasing stack |
| Min Stack | Auxiliary stack for minimums |

---

## 4. Interview Questions

**Q: Stack vs Queue?**
A: Stack: LIFO, Queue: FIFO. Stack uses push/pop, Queue uses offer/poll.

**Q: Implement Min Stack with O(1) getMin?**
A: Use two stacks - one for values, one for tracking minimums at each level.
